_comment: Native overrides: recompiled guest functions replaced by host C.
This is the ONE place an override is declared. tools/gen_overrides.py
turns it into both halves -- the --isolate list that puts each function in
its own translation unit, and the -Wl,--wrap flags that redirect its call
sites -- because ld's --wrap only intercepts calls that cross an object
file. An override whose function shares a chunk with its caller is bound at
compile time: it links, reports nothing, and never fires. The Xbox side
lost two call sites and an entire observer to exactly that, which is why
the two halves are generated from one file rather than maintained by hand.
The recompiled body is NOT deleted. --wrap keeps it linked and callable as
__real_<name>, so an override can defer to the original and the two stay
Each entry: module, ep (hex string), symbol (the emitted C name), why
and optionally returns: "void" -- which switches off the
return-value gate for that one override and therefore has to be
justified in `why` by naming the CALL SITES that were checked to
overwrite EAX before reading it. The gate exists because the DirectX
override was written void, was not, and made the game branch on

why: Controller-default button callback retained for every event and preset except activating context 1.

FUN_0061dc10 creates Defaults 1/2/3 and supplies contexts 0/1/2. Context 0 remains the shipped keyboard table; context 1 is routed to the verified Xbox binding owner. The callback return is ignored by all three FUN_0061dc10 registrations: it is invoked through the menu callback ABI for side effects, and the caller does not read EAX.
Narrow label adapter for the controller editor's literal Defaults 1 and Defaults 2 fallbacks.

All other localization keys and fallbacks defer to the retained body. Matching the exact fallback strings confines the change to the two buttons built by FUN_0061dc10 while preserving the game's language lookup behavior elsewhere.
The PC settings/default-binding loader, retained and post-hooked.
The real body loads all keyboard/user bindings first. The native
post-hook then installs the bindable Xbox-release preset into the
game's pad-priority slot through retained FUN_006297a0, but only if
the profile has no pad mapping at all. Existing mappings are user
state and are never overwritten. The hotswap pump calls the same
sync path and removes only unchanged port-owned rows on disconnect.
tests/test_xbox_defaults.c calls this shipping wrapper and proves
the retained body runs, 17 exact rows land, repeat sync is idempotent,
disconnect removes them, and one custom row blocks the whole preset.
The game's DirectX 9.0c presence check (issue #18).
It CoCreateInstances a version-reporter COM object and, when that
fails, shows 'DirectX not found' and quits. On this host the failure
is truthful: there is no DirectX, no COM registry, and nothing
implements that interface.
It is overridden rather than satisfied because the question is not
one this port can answer honestly in the affirmative and does not
need to: the renderer is being written natively, so DirectX's
presence is irrelevant to whether the game can draw. The two
alternatives were both worse. Setting Settings\DXChecked=1 makes the
game cache a check that never passed and walk into LoadLibraryA of
d3d9.dll. Returning a fabricated S_OK from CoCreateInstance hands the
game an interface pointer to a vtable that does not exist.
The override reports the substitution once, so a run never silently
appears to have passed a check that was actually skipped.
The frame-cap removal hook (X2_UNPACED), and ONLY when that is set.
The game paces itself: the frame function stores a minimum frame time
(1/30 or 1/60) into its app object at +0x18 at its own top, and then busy-
waits at 0x00401ff0 until that much has elapsed. Zeroing the cap removes
the cap without touching the clock, so everything still sees the time it
actually took -- scaling the clock would make a test that passes at 10x
say nothing about the game.
It has to be written BETWEEN the store and the limiter, and the only host
code that runs in that window is this: the limiter's own first
instruction, CALL 0x0055b610, the timer-singleton accessor. Writing at
Present instead was tried and does nothing -- Present happens LATER in the
frame than the limiter, so the value is overwritten before it is read.
Without X2_UNPACED this defers to the original and changes nothing.
igConversationManager::launchScript -- ported, not replaced.
Issue #63: the tutorial's opening conversation ends without ever
running the script its last response names, so the level's opening
act never happens and the party is eliminated unopposed. The
conversation state machine is small and its record layout is fully
named by the XMLB it is parsed from, so these functions are WRITTEN
in C (src/native/conversation.c) rather than probed as translated
bodies -- a breakpoint on a recompiled body answers what the
translation did, which is a different question from what the game
does.
This one binds the conversation's two actors into the script manager,
calls its by-name launch (vtable +0x3c = FUN_004a1320) and clears the
actors again. It returns the launch's bool in AL.
record::runScripts -- scriptCommand then scriptFile, each launched
only when its first byte is not NUL, which is exactly what the
original's one-byte REPE CMPSB against "" asks. Part of the
conversation port; see 0x00455600.
Declared void: the original sets no return value, and all three call sites (0x0045b1ad, 0x0045b796, 0x0045bcac) overwrite EAX before reading it -- checked, not assumed.
bitmap::resetEligible -- *p = ~*p, then clear bits 6..31. Its callers
zero the word first, so the result is 0x3F; it is ported literally
rather than as that constant, because the constant is a property of
the caller and would stop being true without saying so. Part of the
conversation port; see 0x00455600.
Declared void: the original sets no return value, and its one call site (0x0045b71b, inside FUN_0045b6d0) overwrites EAX before reading it.
record::nextLine -- runs the record's conditionScript, then returns
the first ELIGIBLE child's id, or 0.
Returning 0 is what ends a conversation, so the two ways of doing it
-- the record has no children at all, and none of its children is
eligible -- are counted apart in the report. Part of the conversation
port; see 0x00455600.
igConversationManager::chooseResponse -- the player picked the Nth
OFFERED response, where the offered array has holes (0xFFFFFFFF) that
N does not count, which is why the loop keeps two indices.
FUN_00458700 is the engine's 'begin this response' and a TRUE return
means it DECLINED; the original then skips applying the response
entirely. Both early exits fall through to FUN_00458410 rather than
returning -- the first draft of this port returned instead, which
would have left the UI a frame stale on every out-of-range choice.
Part of the conversation port; see 0x00455600.
Declared void: the original sets no return value, and its one call site -- the vtable +0x18 call at 0x0045d3bc -- is followed by PUSH EBP, so nothing reads EAX.
igConversationManager::update -- the per-frame conversation update,
the function that decides everything: whether a chosen response is
applied, whether the conversation ends, whether the accept button
advances it, and how the highlight moves.
It was left un-ported once because its subtitle-draw block could not
be read off the disassembly. That was the wrong answer -- it leaves
the translated original in place forever -- so the capability to
capture it was built instead (recomp.py emit --record, I050). The
capture showed what the listing hid: 0x0067217c is __ftol and takes
its argument on the X87 STACK, consuming nothing from the integer
stack, so the five PUSHes around it belong to the NEXT call and one
ADD ESP,0x24 cleans all nine at the end. The block draws a 32x32
"$MENU_ACCEPT" prompt -- the conversation's own button prompt.
Declared void: the original sets no return value, and it is reached
only through the conversation vtable slot +0x0c, whose call sites
discard EAX.
The capture is also the acceptance test: over 221 passes, 156 take
the early-out at 26 instructions, 64 the full path at 321, and
exactly one -- the pass that chose a response -- 342.
igConversationManager::isVisible -- (flags >> 1) & 1, in AL only.
This is the predicate the per-frame update tests before doing
anything, so it decides whether the conversation is live at all.
Part of the conversation port; see 0x00455600.
igConversationManager::isSpeaking -- (flags >> 2) & 1, in AL only.
Part of the conversation port; see 0x00455600.
The physical-input name boundary used by action prompts.
FUN_00619e30 resolves an action to a binding, passes its device kind
and code to this function, and formats the returned name as [%s].
The original maps gamepad kinds 3..0xc and button codes 0x15..0x31
to textual Btn N names; its signed-axis table identifies code 5 as
Z+ and 6 as Z-, which are left/right trigger in the DirectInput
layout measured and implemented by dinput_pad.c. Codes 0x11..0x14
are the four POV directions.
The override returns the port font's corresponding one-byte glyph
only when that gamepad slot is SDL-classified Xbox 360/One and the
generated font pack is active. It defers to the retained original
body for keyboards, non-Xbox pads, unknown codes, and LS/RS (which
have no authored SVG), so it cannot turn a missing icon into a blank
prompt. It reuses the original function's guest static name buffer
rather than truncating a 64-bit host string pointer.
tests/test_pad_glyphs.c calls this exact shipping wrapper and checks
its RET 8 stack contract, return pointer and bytes, both controller
families, an unsupported code, and the font-pack-disabled gate.
Gap::Core::igWin32ReportBox::doModal -- the engine's error dialog
(issue #47).
The original builds a DLGTEMPLATE by hand and runs it through
DialogBoxIndirectParamA, measuring its text with DrawTextA. That is
the USER32 dialog family -- DialogBoxIndirectParamA, DrawTextA,
GetDlgItem, SendDlgItemMessageA, EndDialog -- none of which this port
implements, and implementing them means writing a dialog manager and
a text renderer for a template nothing else uses.
So the DIALOG is replaced and the MESSAGE is not. SDL shows a real
modal with the same title and the same buttons, and returns the same
codes the guest's dialog procedure returns (3 Exit, 4 Debug,
5 Ignore, 6 Ignore-always), so the caller cannot tell the difference.
The 'Do not tell me again' CHECKBOX becomes the fourth button,
because SDL's modal has no checkbox and the two outcomes are what the
checkbox actually selects between.
It is an override rather than an implementation of the dialog family
for the same reason the DirectX check is one: the question is not
'can this host draw a Win32 dialog' but 'what did the engine want to
tell the player, and what did the player answer'.
A run with no screen (--no-window) answers Ignore and says so, naming
the button -- it is the only answer that neither kills the process
nor invents a debugger.
